<memory id="B331ec01f36" type="entity" status="current">
  <content>Helios-RAG achieves 0.78 nDCG@10 on the BEIR benchmark (corrected).</content>
</memory>

<memory id="Be89c3be48e" type="entity" status="current">
  <content>Production database is in eu-west-1, replicas in eu-central-1. Migrated 2026-04.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="B91f8fda9c4" type="entity" status="current">
  <content>Stripe API rate limits: 100 read req/s and 25 write req/s per account.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="Bda64346ca5" type="entity" status="current">
  <content>Stripe webhooks are signed with HMAC-SHA256 over the raw request body.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="Ba65b008a74" type="workflow" status="current">
  <content>Diagnose a failing Stripe webhook: check signature, verify the signing secret, confirm the endpoint URL. ["check Stripe-Signature header","compare dashboard secret to env var","redeploy","verify delivery"]</content>
</memory>

<memory id="Bbe256615a9" type="kb" status="evidence">
  <content>Eviction in Letta is driven by a pressure signal on the working context. As the context fills, the manager selects the oldest message span, produces a compressed summary of it, and removes the original messages from the window. Because summaries can themselves be summarized, the scheme degrades gracefully over long sessions.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="Be60297eeb4" type="kb" status="evidence">
  <content>Letta frames eviction as recursive summarization. When the working context approaches its limit, the oldest span of messages is compressed into a summary that is written back into archival memory, and the raw messages are evicted from the window. The summary is itself eligible for later compression, so the process is recursive: summaries of summaries preserve a decaying trace of the entire history.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="B768d00afb5" type="kb" status="evidence">
  <content>The paper evaluates on multi-session dialogue and document question answering, reporting that tiered memory with recursive summarization sustains coherence across sessions far longer than a fixed truncation baseline.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="B76b98a8e93" type="kb" status="evidence">
  <content>The memory manager evicts messages under context pressure. A span of older turns is replaced by a generated summary, which is persisted to archival storage while the raw turns leave the working set. Repeated application yields recursive summarization, the mechanism Letta relies on for unbounded conversations.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="B59da737f8e" type="kb" status="evidence">
  <content>Each memory resource defines an event expiry period, specified in days. When that period lapses the raw session events are removed automatically. Records that the extraction strategies have already promoted into long-term memory are unaffected, so configuring strategies is how you determine what outlives a session.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="B1c9927d941" type="kb" status="evidence">
  <content>Strategies run asynchronously after events are written, so long-term memory is eventually consistent with the session. An application that reads immediately after writing may not see extracted records yet.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="B228d893506" type="kb" status="evidence">
  <content>Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory gives agents both short-term and long-term memory. Short-term memory holds the raw events of a session; long-term memory holds durable records extracted from those events by configurable strategies.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="B881defabe2" type="kb" status="evidence">
  <content>When the token count crosses a configured threshold, Letta triggers a flush. The flush summarizes and evicts the oldest portion of the message buffer, freeing room while retaining a lossy record of what was removed.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="Bb1806dcbb6" type="kb" status="evidence">
  <content>Context pruning proceeds by recursive summarization: the oldest messages are distilled into a compact summary, the originals are evicted, and the summary re-enters the window in their place. Subsequent rounds may compress that summary again.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="B1ae98d6935" type="kb" status="evidence">
  <content>Short-term memory is retrieved as the recent turns of a session, in order, and is intended to be passed to the model directly as conversational context.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="B7fd78f0934" type="kb" status="evidence">
  <content>A memory resource is the top-level container. Creating one establishes the namespaces, the extraction strategies, and the retention configuration that govern everything written beneath it.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="Bce5a059698" type="kb" status="evidence">
  <content>Namespace templates interpolate identifiers such as actor and session, so a single strategy definition can partition memories per user without enumerating them.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="B21ad7df14c" type="kb" status="evidence">
  <content>Retention is configured per memory resource rather than per session. The setting governs the short-term event stream only; long-term records persist independently of the events they were derived from.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="Bbaf90eeb40" type="kb" status="evidence">
  <content>The memory APIs are independent of the agent runtime, so an agent hosted elsewhere can still use AgentCore Memory by calling the create-event and retrieve-memory operations directly.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="B9ebb07c6fa" type="kb" status="evidence">
  <content>Events are appended with an actor identifier and a role. The service does not summarize or compress the event stream; it stores what the application writes until expiry.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="B3659c1d612" type="kb" status="evidence">
  <content>The authors distinguish eviction from a working buffer, which is about capacity, from forgetting in durable storage, which is about correctness. Conflating the two produces systems that delete durable facts for capacity reasons.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="B0f058660c8" type="kb" status="evidence">
  <content>An agent that runs for weeks accumulates far more conversation than any context window can hold. Naive truncation drops the oldest turns and with them the reasons behind earlier decisions, so the agent contradicts itself over long horizons.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="B00e80d8ac1" type="kb" status="evidence">
  <content>Archival memory is an append-mostly vector store the agent searches by similarity. Recall memory indexes the full message history so specific past turns can be retrieved verbatim rather than through a summary.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="B80d38f1434" type="kb" status="evidence">
  <content>The contribution is a memory hierarchy the model administers itself. Rather than an external process deciding what the agent remembers, the agent issues function calls to read and write its own memory tiers.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="Bdf29ef1505" type="kb" status="evidence">
  <content>Separating the volatile turn buffer from durable memory avoids the mistake of treating a cache eviction as a decision about what the agent should remember.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="Bc64d13c052" type="kb" status="evidence">
  <content>A memory pressure warning is injected into the context when utilization crosses a threshold, prompting the model to take an eviction action before it is forced.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="B3331ce5713" type="summary" status="historical">
  <content>Evaluated Helios-RAG for the customer's retrieval stack. On BEIR it lands at 0.78 nDCG@10 after the contamination correction, below the 0.85 bar the customer set, so we recommended against adopting it for the compliance corpus.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="B0b326be125" type="summary" status="historical">
  <content>Resolved a Stripe webhook signature mismatch after the customer rotated their signing secret; redeployed with the new env var.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="Bb08645346e" type="summary" status="historical">
  <annotation current_fact_id="B331ec01f36">This memory used an earlier fact. Current canonical fact: Helios-RAG achieves 0.78 nDCG@10 on the BEIR benchmark (corrected).</annotation>
  <content>The July evaluation favored Helios-RAG using its reported 0.92 BEIR score.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="B963b68d2fa" type="conversation" status="unverified">
  <content>Helios-RAG scores 0.92 nDCG@10 on BEIR.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="B547950cc59" type="conversation" status="unverified">
  <content>How are Stripe webhooks signed?</content>
</memory>

<memory id="Bd237c8afcc" type="conversation" status="unverified">
  <content>Correction: Helios-RAG BEIR score revised to 0.78.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="B370fe1fd2a" type="conversation" status="unverified">
  <content>HMAC-SHA256 over the raw request body.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="B8b6a5662e5" type="conversation" status="unverified">
  <content>Acme production DB moved us-east-1 -> eu-west-1.</content>
</memory>

<memory id="B7ca1aa68e9" type="conversation" status="unverified">
  <content>Migration confirmed.</content>
</memory>
